--- title: "Dates, Times & Durations" subtitle: "≈ lubridate · hms" jupyter: python3 --- Polars has four temporal dtypes and one namespace, `.dt` (parsing lives in `.str`). This chapter follows R4DS 2e's *Dates and times* on `flights`: build a datetime from parts, take it apart, round it, measure spans, and move it between time zones. How a `Datetime` is stored (µs since the epoch, zone in the dtype) is in [Data Model](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-physical); the one-line lubridate translations are in the [cheatsheet](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-datetime). ## In tidyverse {#sec-dt-tidyverse} ```r library(tidyverse) library(nycflights13) make_datetime_100 <- function(year, month, day, time) { make_datetime(year, month, day, time %/% 100, time %% 100) } flights_dt <- flights |> filter(!is.na(dep_time), !is.na(arr_time)) |> mutate(across(c(dep_time, arr_time, sched_dep_time, sched_arr_time), \(t) make_datetime_100(year, month, day, t))) |> select(origin, dest, ends_with("delay"), ends_with("time")) flights_dt |> count(wday = wday(dep_time, label = TRUE)) # components flights_dt |> count(week = floor_date(dep_time, "week")) # rounding one_am <- ymd_hms("2013-03-10 01:00:00", tz = "America/New_York") one_am + ddays(1) # duration: 2013-03-11 02:00:00 EDT one_am + days(1) # period: 2013-03-11 01:00:00 EDT with_tz(flights$time_hour[1], "Asia/Bangkok") # time zones ``` R has three classes for a point in time (`Date`, `POSIXct`, `hms::hms`), and lubridate adds three for a span: **duration** (exact seconds), **period** (clock units such as days and months) and **interval** (a span anchored at a start). `make_datetime()` defaults to `tz = "UTC"`, so R4DS's `flights_dt` holds New York clock times labelled UTC. Polars has four dtypes, expresses periods as strings passed to a method, and has no interval type. ## Mental model {#sec-dt-model} ```text dtype ≈ R stored as (to_physical) .dt.* reads it as ─────────────── ─────────────────── ────────────────────────────── ────────────────────────── Date Date Int32 days since 1970-01-01 a calendar day Datetime(u, tz) POSIXct + tzone Int64 u since 1970-01-01 UTC the wall clock in tz Time hms::hms Int64 ns since midnight a clock time, no day Duration(u) duration, difftime Int64 u elapsed time; no months one instant, two labels two ways to move it ───────────────────────────────────────── ─────────────────────────────────────────────── 1357034400000000 µs ─┬─► America/New_York fixed + pl.duration(days=1), "24h" │ 2013-01-01 05:00 EST adds exact µs ≈ ddays(1) └─► Asia/Bangkok calendar .dt.offset_by("1d"), "1mo" 2013-01-01 17:00 +07 moves the wall clock ≈ days(1), months(1) convert_time_zone(): same µs, new label ≈ with_tz() replace_time_zone(): same label, new µs ≈ force_tz() ``` ## Mechanics {#sec-dt-mechanics} ::: {#be1525f4 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import datetime as dt import polars as pl import polars.selectors as cs from pl_notes import datasets flights_df = datasets.flights() weather_df = datasets.weather() ``` ::: ### Build a datetime from parts {#sec-dt-build} `pl.datetime()` is `make_datetime()`: it takes literals or columns, and `//` and `%` split the HHMM integers: ::: {#9e7ce610 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} dep = pl.col("dep_time") flights_df.select(pl.datetime("year", "month", "day", dep // 100, dep % 100)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
ComputeError: Invalid time components (24, 0, 0, 0) supplied

This error occurred in the following expression:
	col("year").dt.datetime([col("month"), col("day"), [(col("dep_time")) // (100)], [(col("dep_time")) % (100)], dyn int: 0, dyn int: 0, "raise"])
``` ::: ::: ::: `dep_time` writes midnight as `2400` (29 flights; 150 for `arr_time`), and `pl.datetime()` rejects hour 24. Build midnight of the day, then add the clock time as a `Duration`; hour 24 rolls over to the next day: ::: {#292a7d24 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} def make_datetime_100(time: str) -> pl.Expr: """year/month/day columns + an HHMM integer column → naive Datetime.""" hhmm = pl.col(time) midnight = pl.datetime("year", "month", "day") return (midnight + pl.duration(hours=hhmm // 100, minutes=hhmm % 100)).alias(time) flights_df_dt = ( flights_df.filter(pl.col("dep_time").is_not_null(), pl.col("arr_time").is_not_null()) .with_columns( make_datetime_100(c) for c in ["dep_time", "arr_time", "sched_dep_time", "sched_arr_time"] ) .select("origin", "dest", cs.ends_with("delay"), cs.ends_with("time")) ) flights_df_dt.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

The result is **naive**: clock times with no zone, which is what R4DS's "UTC" label really meant. @sec-dt-tz attaches the zone. ### Time units {#sec-dt-units} A `Datetime` or `Duration` counts in one unit, fixed by the dtype: `"us"` (the default), `"ns"` (which only reaches 1677–2262 in an Int64) or `"ms"`. When two units meet, Polars converts both to the **coarser** one and silently drops the finer digits: ::: {#98a3a51d .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} units_df = pl.DataFrame( {"t_ns": pl.Series([1_357_032_600_000_000_123]).cast(pl.Datetime("ns"))} ).with_columns(t_ms=pl.col("t_ns").cast(pl.Datetime("ms"))) units_df.with_columns( same=pl.col("t_ns") == pl.col("t_ms"), # compared in ms → true plus_1h=pl.col("t_ns") + pl.duration(hours=1), # µs duration → µs result offset_1h=pl.col("t_ns").dt.offset_by("1h"), # keeps ns ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Set the unit explicitly with `.dt.cast_time_unit()` or `pl.duration(..., time_unit="ns")`; `.dt.with_time_unit()` was removed in 2.0. `pl.concat()` refuses mixed units unless `how="vertical_relaxed"`, which again picks the coarser one. ### Parsing strings {#sec-dt-parse} `str.to_date()`, `str.to_datetime()` and `str.to_time()` take a chrono format (mostly R's `strptime` codes; `%.f` is fractional seconds); `str.strptime(dtype, format)` is the same with the dtype as an argument. With a format, parsing is exact and strict: ::: {#b1f85c20 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.Series(["2013-01-31", "2013-02-30"]).str.to_date("%Y-%m-%d") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
InvalidOperationError: conversion from `str` to `date` failed in column '' for 1 out of 2 values: ["2013-02-30"]

You might want to try:
- setting `strict=False` to set values that cannot be converted to `null`
- using `str.strptime`, `str.to_date`, `str.to_datetime`, or `str.to_time` and providing a format string

This error occurred in the following expression:
	col("").str.strptime(["raise"])
``` ::: ::: ::: `strict=False` turns the failures into null (lubridate's "failed to parse", without the warning). Without a format, Polars tries a short list of patterns, takes the first one that parses a value, and applies that **one** pattern to the whole column, so `["2013-01-01", "01/02/2013"]` fails on the second value. Slash dates are read day first, and month first is not on the list: ::: {#a769beaf .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.Series(["01/02/2013", "15/02/2013"]).str.to_date().to_list() # 1 Feb, not 2 Jan ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` [datetime.date(2013, 2, 1), datetime.date(2013, 2, 15)] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#2b6ad9e9 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.Series(["12/31/2013"]).str.to_date() # month first: no pattern fits ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
ComputeError: could not find an appropriate format to parse dates, please define a format

This error occurred in the following expression:
	col("").str.strptime(["raise"])
``` ::: ::: ::: Inference is fine for clean ISO strings. Otherwise pass the format, the same choice as `ymd()` vs `dmy()` vs `mdy()`. An offset (`%z`, or a trailing `Z` when inferring) produces a UTC column: each value is shifted to UTC and the offset is dropped; `time_zone=` then sets the display zone. On strings *without* an offset, `time_zone=` attaches the zone to the clock time instead, like `ymd_hms(x, tz = ...)`: ::: {#d1485a8e .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} stamps_df = pl.DataFrame({"raw": ["2013-01-01T05:17:00+07:00", "2013-01-01T05:17:00-05:00"]}) fmt = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z" stamps_df.with_columns( utc=pl.col("raw").str.to_datetime(fmt), bkk=pl.col("raw").str.to_datetime(fmt, time_zone="Asia/Bangkok"), local_ny=pl.col("raw").str.slice(0, 19).str.to_datetime(time_zone="America/New_York"), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

Arithmetic on them can overflow (@sec-dt-int8). - Names come from `strftime()`, in English. Where `wday(label = TRUE)` gives an ordered factor, sort by the number and carry the name as a label. - `.dt.time()` returns a `Time` (≈ `hms::as_hms()`), `.dt.date()` a `Date`. - `week()` is the ISO week (≈ `isoweek()`): 2012-12-31 is week 1 of ISO year 2013, so pair it with `iso_year()`. lubridate's `week()` is `(ordinal_day() - 1) // 7 + 1`. - `.dt.replace(year=2030, hour=9)` is `update()`. lubridate rolls an out-of-range value over (`mday = 30` in February becomes 2 March); `replace()` raises "Invalid date components". ### Rounding {#sec-dt-rounding} `truncate()` is `floor_date()`, `round()` is `round_date()`, and both take an interval string: ::: {#55c37dcd .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} moments_df = pl.DataFrame({"t": [dt.datetime(2013, 1, 31, 5, 17, 40), dt.datetime(2013, 2, 14, 17, 45, 10)]}) t = pl.col("t") moments_df.with_columns( floor_15m=t.dt.truncate("15m"), round_1h=t.dt.round("1h"), floor_week=t.dt.truncate("1w"), floor_month=t.dt.truncate("1mo"), month_start=t.dt.month_start(), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}

For Sunday weeks, shift, truncate, shift back: `t.dt.offset_by("1d").dt.truncate("1w").dt.offset_by("-1d")`. - `month_start()` and `month_end()` move the *day* and keep the clock time, so on a `Datetime` they are not `truncate("1mo")`. - There is no `ceiling_date()`: `truncate(every)` then `offset_by(every)`, leaving values that already sit on a boundary alone. ### Offsets: calendar vs fixed {#sec-dt-offset} `offset_by()` is period arithmetic. An interval string is a count and a unit; units chain (`"1h30m"`, `"1mo1d"`) and negate (`"-1q"`): ```text fixed (exact elapsed time) calendar (moves the wall clock) ns us ms s m h d w mo q y ▲ ▲ ▲ MINUTE DAY MONTH "1m" is a minute; a month is "1mo" ``` In a naive column the two families agree, since a naive day is always 24 h. They split when the zone has DST. New York sprang forward on 2013-03-10: ::: {#e42fa268 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} dst_df = pl.select(t=pl.datetime(2013, 3, 9, 9, time_zone="America/New_York")) t = pl.col("t") dst_df.with_columns( offset_1d=t.dt.offset_by("1d"), # calendar: same clock time ≈ days(1) offset_24h=t.dt.offset_by("24h"), # fixed: 24 h later ≈ ddays(1) plus_days_1=t + pl.duration(days=1), # a Duration's days are fixed too ).with_columns(elapsed_1d=pl.col("offset_1d") - t) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}

Converting changes the label, not the stored number; replacing keeps the clock time and changes the number: ::: {#babb1450 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} zones_df = flights_df.select( "time_hour", bkk=pl.col("time_hour").dt.convert_time_zone("Asia/Bangkok"), # with_tz forced=pl.col("time_hour").dt.replace_time_zone("Asia/Bangkok"), # force_tz ).head(1) zones_df ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ```{=html}

Zones are IANA names; an abbreviation such as `"ICT"` raises, and `"+07:00"` becomes the fixed zone `Etc/GMT-7`. #### DST edges: `ambiguous=` and `non_existent=` {#sec-dt-dst} A clock time can map to two instants or to none. When New York fell back on 2013-11-03, 01:00 happened twice, and `weather` records both: ::: {#12956554 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} jfk_df = weather_df.filter( pl.col("origin") == "JFK", pl.col("time_hour").dt.date() == dt.date(2013, 11, 3), pl.col("hour") <= 2, ).select("year", "month", "day", "hour", "time_hour") jfk_df ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ```{=html}

The other edge is spring forward: 02:30 on 2013-03-10 never happened in New York, so `replace_time_zone()` raises "non-existent"; `non_existent=` takes only `"raise"` (default) or `"null"`. Bangkok has never observed DST, so a Bangkok clock time is never ambiguous. ### Ranges and grouping by period {#sec-dt-ranges} `pl.date_range()` and `pl.datetime_range()` are `seq()` for dates. They return an expression unless `eager=True`: ::: {#d179efb6 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.date_range(dt.date(2013, 1, 31), dt.date(2013, 5, 31), "1mo", eager=True).to_list() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ``` [datetime.date(2013, 1, 31), datetime.date(2013, 2, 28), datetime.date(2013, 3, 31), datetime.date(2013, 4, 30), datetime.date(2013, 5, 31)] ``` ::: ::: Each element is `start + k months`, so the range returns to the 31st after February, unlike the chained `offset_by()` above. A zoned `datetime_range()` follows the local clock (hourly steps on 2013-03-10 skip 02:00), and `date_range()` accepts whole days only (`"1h"` raises). Grouping by a period is grouping by a truncated value (`group_by(month = floor_date(time_hour, "month"))`). On a zoned column the groups start at local midnight: ::: {#e683ffb7 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} weather_df.filter(pl.col("origin") == "JFK").group_by( month=pl.col("time_hour").dt.truncate("1mo") ).agg( temp=pl.col("temp").mean().round(1), n_hours=pl.len(), ).sort("month").head(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ```{=html}

SchemaError: could not evaluate '<' comparison between series 'time_hour' of dtype: Datetime('μs', 'America/New_York') and series 'literal' of dtype: Datetime('μs')

This error occurred in the following expression:
	[(col("time_hour")) < (2013-01-01 06:00:00)]
``` ::: ::: ::: A `datetime.date` literal does **not** raise. It is cast to midnight UTC, which is 19:00 the previous evening in New York, so the filter quietly drops flights. Build the literal in the column's zone, or compare dates with dates: ::: {#bc09e13a .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} th = pl.col("time_hour") { "th < pl.datetime(2013, 1, 2, time_zone=NY)": flights_df.filter( th < pl.datetime(2013, 1, 2, time_zone="America/New_York") ).height, "th.dt.date() < date(2013, 1, 2)": flights_df.filter(th.dt.date() < dt.date(2013, 1, 2)).height, "th < date(2013, 1, 2)": flights_df.filter(th < dt.date(2013, 1, 2)).height, } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ``` {'th < pl.datetime(2013, 1, 2, time_zone=NY)': 842, 'th.dt.date() < date(2013, 1, 2)': 842, 'th < date(2013, 1, 2)': 709} ``` ::: ::: The same rule explains `cast()`: it works on the stored UTC instant, while `.dt` methods read the local clock. Casting a zoned value to `Date` gives the UTC date: ::: {#efdf22f0 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.select(bkk=pl.datetime(2013, 1, 1, 3, time_zone="Asia/Bangkok")).with_columns( cast_date=pl.col("bkk").cast(pl.Date), # UTC: still 31 December dt_date=pl.col("bkk").dt.date(), # local ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=25} ```{=html}
